activity.title: I’ve always held high expectations for myself, but looking back at where this journey began at 17, I am incredibly proud of how those expectations became a reality. For me, college wasn't a straight line. I wasn't afraid to pivot early on to find the perfect fit, transferring to Oregon State University and exploring international perspectives in Singapore. Every step was about raising the bar. Now I’ve reached the next checkpoint: I have officially graduated from OSU with a B.S. in Business Analytics (Cum Laude) and received the Award for Outstanding Achievement in Business Analytics, an honor awarded to just 3 graduating students in the major this year. I knew I wanted to leave a real impact here, and I’m walking away having accomplished exactly what I set out to do: Served as Chief Marketing Officer for BeaverHacks, driving marketing strategy to scale it into the largest hackathon in Oregon with nearly 500 attendees. Awarded a Certificate of Excellence as President of the Business Analytics Club, and drove community engagement as the PR Officer for the Taekwondo Club. Won multiple developer prizes at hackathons, analyzed real-world data funnels, and traveled to San Francisco with an incredible group of driven peers where I attended a major cybersecurity conference and an array of tech events. I’m happy to say that my team started a movement and I expect it to live on among those who succeed me. Every pivot was an investment in building a versatile, high-impact skill set. Thank you to the incredible mentors, friends, and family who stood by me as I chased down these goals. I am officially #OpenToWork and looking for full-time opportunities in Business Analytics, Data Analysis, or Growth/Marketing Analytics. If your team is looking for a strategic, data-driven builder who thrives on high standards, let’s connect! #Graduation #OregonState #BusinessAnalytics #DataAnalytics #TechLeadership #ClassOf2026

Two years ago, I had a dream. A dream that we could build something that would change people's lives for the better. Every moment of my life for the last 2 years has been dedicated to that mission. The numbers speak for themselves: nearly 500 attendees, 70 volunteers, $20,000 in prizes, backed by incredible sponsors and a community that believed in us before it was certain. We've made an impact, not just at Oregon State, but across the Pacific Northwest. Owen Krause , Caleb Chia , Violette Davis, Joshua Chilango . They're family. They stood by me through situations most people could never face. The sleepless nights, the early mornings, driving 10+ hours down to San Francisco to secure sponsors (with no plan whatsoever). They believed in the vision when no one else did. I asked them to sacrifice so much, with no proof that it would work out, and they showed up every time, because they had the same dream. To the rest of my team — my officers, my devs, my interns: thank you for trusting me. The goals I set, the dreams I have — they aren't realistic. They're ambitious. But that's what makes winning so worth it. Because even when it seemed impossible, it was your faith that brought us this far. Thank you to our industry partners, NVIDIA , Google , C1 , MarkIII , and Trimble Inc. To every judge, volunteer, and staff member, thank you for giving your time and expertise to make this real. To Oregon State Athletics , I walked past Reser Stadium every day for two years on my way to campus, and every day, I knew I had to host our event in the Toyota club. Thank you for helping me bring that dream to life. To Melissa Ward , Forrest Masters , Steve Niemi , Peter Rizk , and Aaron Babcock : every email thread, every text, every last-minute meeting. You were in the trenches with me every single day, fighting to build something meaningful for our community. To those who are scared to start: never let anyone tell you what's not possible. Because two years ago, the Hackathon Club was a small online club nobody had heard of. Today, it's BeaverHacks , Oregon’s Largest Hackathon. So many people told me it was impossible, that OSU simply didn’t have what it took. But to that I say, what’s impossible today will be the reality of tomorrow. I’ll see you all next year at BeaverHacks 2027. Let’s keep building tomorrow together.

joining the BeaverHacks team my freshman year was the best decision I made in college. we started with no playbook and a stupid amount of ambition. going from 0 to 1 meant cold emailing sponsors who never replied, running events nobody showed up to, and figuring out stuff with no guide like how to transfer and distribute 300 burritos. we took a lot of risks. some failed miserably. in fact, last year Havel Konda and I covered thousands out of pocket when the club went into debt. but sometimes the stars would just align and we'd do the impossible. three years later, we ran the biggest student hackathon in Oregon. 450+ registrations and projects that genuinely blew me away. extremely grateful for Violette Davis who is graduating this year. building BeaverHacks means more to me than I can put into words and you and and the rest of the team made it possible.

BeaverHacks 2026 kicks off in less than 24 hours, and we’re excited to bring together hundreds of students, builders, and innovators for an unforgettable experience. Huge thanks to our sponsors and partners for making this possible, including Steve Niemi and NVIDIA AI We’ll see you all very soon…

🏆 We won the Ghost track at the Deep Agents Hackathon by building an AI-powered data collection and labeling tool. My teammates Owen Krause , Havel Konda and Caleb Chia and I competed in a non-collegiate hackathon inside the Amazon Web Services (AWS) Loft in San Francisco, alongside industry professionals. Our project, CRWL, is an autonomous web research tool. Drop a topic. Parallel Claude agents crawl the web from every angle, coordinate through a shared Postgres database, and hand you back a clean labeled dataset. The core idea: agents don’t need a central controller. They synchronize through shared state. Ghost gave us a managed Postgres instance in a single command, and the rest fell into place. The perfect way to close out the week. Thank you to Tiger Data (creators of TimescaleDB) for hosting the track. 🔗 Check out CRWL: GitHub → https://lnkd.in/gsfNpApZ Devpost → https://lnkd.in/g2DFF3E6

Some people see spring break as time to relax by stepping away from tech, but I disagree, I relax by diving further into it. That's why I optimized my entire spring break around a visit to my hometown, San Francisco, the most technical city in the world. Fellow BeaverHacks organizers Havel Konda , Caleb Chia , Owen Krause and I drove down together. Here's how the week actually went: I found free RSAC 2026 passes through a Tailscale event listed on Luma . Over the next few days that unlocked many opportunities. We sat in on panels and keynotes from many speakers, such as the CEO of SentinelOne , heard a former Google security lead walk through how his team used AI-powered offensive tooling to red-team organizations in real time, and attended a dinner where we got to hear from cybersecurity experts on where AI attacks are actually heading. On the expo floor we got to talk to teams from tons of amazing companies like GitLab and ServiceNow . We attended a Stanford University seminar on AI agents and payments, to hear Illia Polosukhin (co-author of the original Transformer paper and founder of NEAR) talk about securing agentic commerce, alongside many other amazing speakers figuring out what the internet looks like in the next five years. We attended a Y Combinator AI Founders Night where we listened to a YC founder talk about how to optimize content creation. We met up with lots of amazing people. Including a founder of a VC startup that's revolutionizing the world of AI companions, and we were able to have insightful conversations with other developers while visiting the Google and Meta HQs. Today I'm closing the week at the Amazon Web Services (AWS) loft for a Deep Agents Hackathon. At the end of the day, I came here and did all these things because I love this. The connections and networking opportunities were a bonus, I'm just happy to be somewhere that feels like home, with people like me. Normally, it feels like we're the only technical enthusiasts around, but this week, everyone around us spoke the same language. (Honorable mention: We checked out the computer history museum and a creative code exhibition. Both were amazing, I recommend both if you get the chance.)
